title: Rejecting extremism
hookLine: scholars have condemned terrorism as against Islam, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi

cards: The letter is addressed to one man, by name: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, who had declared himself caliph of the group called ISIS, and to the fighters who followed him. Not to the world, not to the press.
It's written in Arabic, in the language of the law he claimed to be applying, and signed by Muslim scholars and leaders from many countries. Its message, point after point, is a single word: no.

teach.b: The Open Letter to al-Baghdadi doesn't shout. It argues, verse by verse, like a teacher marking an exam. Issuing religious rulings without the learning they require is forbidden.
Killing the innocent is forbidden. Killing emissaries is forbidden, and so killing journalists and aid workers is too. Torture is forbidden.

Declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, when they haven't declared it themselves, is forbidden. And fighting in Islam has rules, a right cause and a right conduct, and isn't permitted without them.
Behind those points sit texts anyone can read.
In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors."
And in Sunan an-Nasa'i the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns against going to extremes in religion, saying, in paraphrase, that people before you were destroyed by it.
The Arabic word is ghuluw: overshooting, going past the mark. Read beside the letter, the hadith names the charge. Not too much religion.
Excess that leaves religion behind. And the letter is one statement among several.

Scholars in different countries have issued their own fatwas and declarations against terrorism, in mosques and in print, public for anyone to read. They say, in their own words, what today's line says in three.

how: Muslim scholars and organizations issue public letters, fatwas and declarations against terrorism, often arguing from the Qur'an and hadith point by point, and imams address the subject in sermons.

o: scholars answering violence in Islam's name from the Qur'an and hadith
governments banning Muslim groups that seem too religious to them
avoiding any extra prayer or fasting beyond the bare minimum

games.q: you're a scholar. a man has declared himself caliph, and his fighters kill journalists and aid workers in your faith's name. what do you do?
o: stay quiet: it isn't your fight.
write to him by name, in Arabic, and answer him point by point from the texts.
issue a short statement in English for the press only.
games.why: the signers of the Open Letter wrote to al-Baghdadi by name, in Arabic, and argued from the Qur'an and hadith that what his group was doing is forbidden.

practice: Bring to mind a headline that used a faith's name for an act of violence; you don't have to replay the images, just notice how the story usually ends there.
Now add the part that rarely gets told: somewhere, a scholar sat down and wrote an answer, with the line from al-Baqarah behind it, begin not hostilities.
If you pray, pray for those harmed in that faith's name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Rejecting extremism. Scholars answering violence done in Islam's name with the Qur'an and hadith, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: excess, overshooting the mark; the word in the hadith warning against extremes in religion.

carryVoice: Your line: scholars said no. Point by point, in their own terms and texts. Until tomorrow.
